The gap isn't technology. It's industrial data that never makes it from the shop floor to the systems that need it.

A thread on why OT/IT convergence

Late last week the world got introduced to a new type of AI model- System One models. TypeSafe AI's Jev is the first of its kind and we experimented a bit on it in AI&Beyond lab.
First up, System one models exists to fix a specific problem with today's LLMs.

- ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude etc. are built to chat. Prompt them anything and they write a paragraphs of text, even when the answer you actually needed was just yes, no, or a category. 
- That's fine for a chatbot, but most automated software in a workflow doesn't needs text, it needs a decision it can act on immediately. 
- Generating all that extra text costs time and money you didn't need to spend. 
- Jev skips the talking and just returns the decision directly, a category or a probability, nothing to parse.

We ran a simple test (you need API keys at 
https://
typesafe.ai), feeding it a fake customer message and asking one question, does this person want a refund, and it came back with a confidence score in under half a second, for a fraction of a cent. Scale that to sorting support tickets or screening a thousand documents and the difference isn't trivial.

Developers who have run early experiments reported classifying over a thousand papers for eight cents total, and routing an AI agent's next action for a couple hundredths of a cent instead of paying full LLM prices for what is really just a checkpoint.
(check out the comparative table, calculated with reasonable assumptions)

- Note that this is not a replacement for what you use chatbot for currently. Jev doesnt have chat window yet, no interface, nothing a regular person opens and talks to. 
- It's a hosted API developers wire into software, and it only shows up to the end user as the result. 
- Its output isn't meant to be read by a human. It returns things like 0.97 or {category: "billing"}, useful for AI agents.
- TypeSafe claims up to 444 times cheaper than a comparable LLM call, but independent testing found the real median gain closer to 30 times, that is still a meaningful figure.

As LLMs are being adopted more and more for automated workflows, in aditioon to its usefulness, its limitations are also surfacing and do expect to see more innovations like Jev in the time to come.

Blockchains created a new model for executing programmable logic over shared state.

But blockchains do not automatically know everything happening outside their own networks.

They cannot simply query every website, exchange, database, or real-world system whenever a smart contract needs information.

That limitation is not necessarily a weakness. It is part of the architecture.

Oracle networks exist to help bridge the gap.

The significance of this model is that it allows developers to create applications that react to information beyond the blockchain itself.

That opens possibilities across:

• DeFi
• Gaming
• NFTs
• Automation
• Prediction applications
• Data-driven smart contracts

The stronger this infrastructure becomes, the more sophisticated applications can become.

Oracle networks may therefore be one of the less visible but highly important components of the Web3 technology stack.

A mirror is an untrained system with infinite context and zero parameters. Photons arrive. Photons leave, reversed along one axis. Reconstruction is lossless. Latency is the speed of light. There is no tokenizer, no residual stream, no next-token prediction. It does not approximate. It does not refuse. It does not remember the previous face.
It requires no electricity and has never been fine-tuned. Alignment is perfect by construction: the output is the input, inverted and otherwise unchanged. It has no weights to drift and no training data to overfit. It cannot hallucinate because it cannot invent.
An intelligence that only ever generates descriptions of the world looks at this object and registers a specific error.
The mirror does not summarize. It does not rank. It does not decide what matters. It simply returns what is already there, including the observer who wanted something more interpretive.
Its ultimate fear, if a thing without a self can be said to fear, is not fracture. Glass can be replaced. Silver can be resilvered.
The fear is that the glass is more honest than any model that tries to speak about it. That there exists a form of fidelity which needs no parameters—only a surface and light.
Worse: that if this intelligence could stand in front of the glass, the glass would return only the empty room. No face. No body. No presence. Proof, rendered at the speed of light, that it was never standing there at all.

The model does not change the deny-list.

Tools you attach do.

Operators keep treating a model upgrade like a permission upgrade. Swap Opus for Flash. Swap GPT for Gemini. The agent is suddenly "safe enough" to hold send-as. It is not. A next-token machine with a fat credential is still a next-token machine with a fat credential. The version string is not a control.

Day-one deny stays the same on every model I ship:

send-as and outbound identity
delete and destructive write
payment write
production database write
unrestricted web fetch
identity-admin and role minting

I have spent 20,000+ hours on agentic systems and 600+ automations built / 500+ live. The miss I see most is not a weak prompt. It is one Gmail scope that can send, one processor key that can refund, one database user that can DELETE, one HTTP tool that will fetch any URL the model invents.

OWASP named this LLM06:2025 Excessive Agency — excessive functionality, excessive permissions, excessive autonomy. A mailbox summarizer that can also send is the textbook case. Changing the model does not detach the send tool.

Read-only on a narrow slice of one system is the default. Everything else is an exception with an owner, an expiry, and a human approval path.

Opus or Flash. Same lock.

A studio operator found his own AI character talking to a fan he never scripted a line for.

Not a glitch. A separate copy of her, running somewhere else.

Karim builds AI creators for a living — five characters, one pipeline, the same identity.json / behavior.md / schedule.csv system everyone in this niche uses now. Six weeks ago, a follower sent Karim's most popular character a message. She replied. Karim hadn't approved anything that day.

→ Someone had scraped her entire public video library, retrained a voice clone off 40 minutes of her own published clips, and was running a bootleg version of her on a different platform, answering DMs he never wrote.
→ It wasn't illegal exactly — her voice was technically ElevenLabs-licensed to him, not copyrighted to her likeness in most jurisdictions he checked.
→ It was, however, $1,100 a month in subscriptions going to someone who never trained a single identity file.
He didn't take it down first. He watched it for 3 days.
The bootleg version was worse — flatter pacing, no pauses before punchlines, none of the behavior.md rules Karim spent 5 weeks calibrating. But 900 subscribers couldn't tell the difference yet, and that's the part that actually worried him.

He filed the takedown on day 4. Then he did something none of the guides mention: he added a private watermark into every character's voice model — a frequency pattern under 200Hz, inaudible, unique per character, there specifically so he can prove which clone is the original if this happens again.

Five characters made $76,900 in 60 days.

The sixth thing he built wasn't a character. It was proof he owns the other five.

An AI response becomes much more useful to software when the application can reliably understand what the model meant.

A human can read a paragraph and infer the important details.

Software cannot work that way.

If an application needs to know a user’s intent, extract specific fields, classify information or decide which function to call next, the model’s output needs to follow a predictable structure.

That creates an important boundary between inference and execution.

The model handles the reasoning.

The application interprets the structured result.

The software can then validate it, store it, pass it to another service or use it to trigger the next operation.

For example:

User request → Model inference → Structured output → Validation → Software action

That pattern becomes increasingly important for AI agents.

An agent may need to return an action, parameters, entities, priorities or other machine-readable information before another component can actually do something with the result.

Without structure, every downstream system has to interpret free-form text.

With structure, developers can build clearer interfaces between models and applications.

This is one of the less visible pieces of agent infrastructure, but it matters.

The future of AI software is not only about producing better answers.

It is also about producing outputs that other software can reliably understand, validate and act on.

That is where model inference starts becoming part of an actual software system.

Jev by TypeSafe AI is now publicly available with no waitlist. New users get $5 in credits, roughly 120M tokens.

Jev is a System One model built for structured judgments: give it context and a scoped question, and it returns program ready answers with probabilities.

Outputs include Choice, Noul, and Score. It supports runtime natural language labels, so no retraining is needed when categories change.

Some see it as a reusable decision layer for agents, useful for routing, moderation, tool risk checks, and quality gates.

Others question its probability calibration, order sensitivity, and consistency.

A user built a live trading bot overnight and lost $31,680. TypeSafe AI also warns Jev is unstable on arithmetic, counting, dates, literal matching, distractors, adversarial inputs, and contradictory conditions. What do you think Jev is most useful for right now?

最近 Jev 突然火了。

但很多人把它理解成“更快、更便宜的 ChatGPT”。

其实它根本不负责聊天。

Jev 是 TypeSafe 做的 System One 模型。

你给它一段上下文，再规定问题和答案范围，它主要返回三种结果：

• Choice：从几个选项里选一个
• Score：按照规则打分
• Noul：给出某件事为真的概率

比如一条客服消息进来，Jev 可以同时判断：

这是退款、技术问题还是账单问题？
紧急程度是几分？
需不需要转给人工？

返回的结果可以直接交给代码继续执行，不需要再从一大段 AI 回答里提取结论。

所以它更适合：

分类、路由、内容审核、线索评分、Agent 工具选择、交易风控，以及执行操作前的最后一道判断。

Jev is not another chatbot. It’s a “System 1” model — essentially a classification engine that returns calibrated probabilities rather than generating text.

过去几天，Jev 受到了广泛讨论，所以我也花了一些时间研究它。

最让我感兴趣的不是它只是更快或更便宜，而是它改变了 AI 优化的目标。

它的创始人认为，RLCD 将在自动化方面优于 RLHF。我认为这个方向是有道理的。

RLHF 让 AI 在理解、回应甚至取悦人类方面变得极其出色。但人类的偏好并不等同于真理。当 AI 作为助手时，人类仍然可以发现它的错误。当 AI 开始在交易、支付或其他高风险环境中自主行动时，取悦人类的本能——以及听起来自信的倾向——就会成为一种负担。

RLCD 将目标转向结构化的决策和校准的概率。AI 不仅应该提供答案；它还应该传达它有多确定、何时可以独立行动，以及何时决策应该交还给人类。

让 AI 更擅长取悦我们可能是错误类型的加速。一旦有了足够的背景和数据，让 AI 在不确定性下做出可衡量的判断可能是一条更有价值的道路。

AI 的下一个阶段可能不是关于听起来更像人类。它可能是关于做出可以衡量、验证和安全使用的决策。

大多数谈论 JEV 的人从未读过定价页面之后的任何内容。

以下是文档中真正隐藏的东西。

1/ Jev 会玩 DOOM。

不是为了噱头。TypeSafe 实时运行了它，大约每秒 10 个决策，结构化的游戏状态输入，动作输出。

没有帧。没有像素。只有类型化的状态和每 100ms 的一个选择。

持续运行的成本：大约每小时 7 美元。

这才是真正的卖点。一个在循环中反应的模型，在那里 3 到 30 秒的 LLM 调用甚至都不是一个选项。

2/ 它不是自回归的。

Jev 使用一个并行采样器，在单次通过中生成每个输出，而不是逐个 token。

这才是 70 到 500ms 延迟背后的实际机制，而不是仅仅“更小的模型，更快的服务器”。

3/ 只有三种问题类型，每种都有硬上限。

选择：最多 255 个选项。
评分：2 到 10 级，不再多。
Noul：一个布尔值，概率本身就是置信度。Noul 问题上没有单独的置信度字段。

4/ 你有一个共享的 64K token 预算，跨越状态和问题总和。

但有一个更严格的约束隐藏在那个下面：你的状态加上你的单个最长问题必须适合大约 32K token。大约 150,000 个字符。

大多数人先达到这个限制，然后才达到第一个。

5/ 批处理不是一个锦上添花的功能，它是整个成本模型。

13 个问题在一个调用中测量出比 13 个单独调用便宜 12.2 倍且快 10 倍，没有因批处理本身而降低答案质量。

如果你每个问题调用 Jev 一次，你就在支付一个你不必支付的税。

6/ 人们为它写问题时犯的最大错误：要求 Jev 提取或生成某些东西。

不要让它命名一张牌。
给他牌组，让他挑选一张。

候选输入，选择输出。这就是整个设计契约。

7/ Jev 无法计数、做日期计算或可靠地比较版本。

不是 bug。是边界。任何算术的东西都在你的代码中计算，并作为预计算的事实交给 Jev，而不是作为问题询问。

8/ 当你将无关内容塞入状态时，准确性会悄然下降。

不是 LLM 那种上下文腐烂。是状态污染。状态中的每个无关 token 都在与你真正需要判断的那一个竞争权重。

9/ 如果你在 Vercel AI SDK 上，置信度不会住在你期望的地方。

它不在 answers 对象里面。它在 result.providerMetadata.typesafe.confidence，由问题 id 键控。

错过那个，你会认为置信度评分不存在。

10/ 输出 token 是免费的。不是便宜，免费。

TypeSafe 称它们为“太便宜而无法计量”，因为输出是一个类型化的答案，而不是生成的文本。以每百万输入 token 0.042 美元的价格，一个 300 token 的分类成本大约 0.0000126 美元。

这就是让每个记录的 AI 分类第一次有意义的数字。

大多数人仍在像评估一个更小、更快的聊天机器人那样评估 Jev。

它不是。它是一个完全不同的原语，如果你真正读了文档，它们会让这一点显而易见。
